title: Timeouts and budgets
summary: Connect versus read timeouts, why the default is dangerous, and why inner layers must give up first.

steps.title: Kinds of timeout
body: Waiting forever is the default in more places than you'd think (Camel's HTTP client has no response limit by
default; .NET's `HttpClient` waits 100 seconds). A slow backend then holds your threads and your callers wait as
long as it does. Set limits deliberately:
- **Connect timeout**: how long to wait to *establish* the connection (TCP, TLS). Short: 1–2 s. A long
connect usually means the host is down or a firewall drops packets.
- **Response / read timeout**: how long to wait for the *answer* once connected. Sized from the backend's
real latency (its p99 plus a margin), e.g. 3 s.
- **Overall deadline**: the total time the whole operation may take, across retries.
In Camel, project-wide settings belong in configuration (and can differ per environment):
```properties
camel.component.http.connect-timeout=2000
camel.component.http.response-timeout=3000
A timeout surfaces as `SocketTimeoutException` (read) or a connect exception: map them to `504` / `502`.

steps.title: Budgets: inner layers give up first
body: Every layer has a timeout, and they must **nest**:
```text
client 10 s  >  gateway 8 s  >  integration 5 s  >  backend call 3 s
If an **outer** layer gives up first, the inner one keeps working on a request nobody is waiting for, the
consumer gets the gateway's generic `504` with no trace id from you, and your logs show a "successful" call
finishing later. With nested budgets, the innermost layer that knows what failed answers first, with a proper
error body.
For retries, the budget is shared: two attempts of 3 s plus backoff must still fit inside the integration's 5 s.
Passing the **remaining** time down (a deadline) is the general solution.

steps.prompt: The gateway's timeout is 5 s, the integration's response timeout is 30 s, and the backend takes 20 s. What does the consumer see?
options: A generic 504 from the gateway after 5 s, while the integration keeps waiting 20 s for an answer nobody will receive
A 504 with the integration's error body after 30 s
steps.explain: Make the integration's limit shorter than the gateway's, so the integration answers first with its own `BACKEND_TIMEOUT` and trace id.

code: Console.WriteLine($"{attempts} attempts fit, worst case {used} ms");
steps.explain: Two 2-second attempts plus one 300 ms pause fit in 5 s; a third attempt would not. Retries must be counted against the budget.

steps.title: Check the timeout budgets
prompt: Write `List<string> CheckBudgets(List<(string Layer, int TimeoutMs)> chain, int marginMs)`. `chain` lists layers from the **outside in** (client first). A timeout of `0` means none is set.
- for each layer with `TimeoutMs == 0`: `"{layer} has no timeout"`;
- for each pair of neighbours where both have timeouts, the inner one must be at most `outer - marginMs`; otherwise
`"{inner} ({t} ms) must be at most {max} ms, inside {outer} ({ot} ms)"`.
Report in chain order (a layer's "no timeout" before the comparison with its inner neighbour).
starter: List<string> CheckBudgets(List<(string Layer, int TimeoutMs)> chain, int marginMs)
solution: List<string> CheckBudgets(List<(string Layer, int TimeoutMs)> chain, int marginMs)
problems.Add($"{inner} ({it} ms) must be at most {t - marginMs} ms, inside {layer} ({t} ms)");
hints: Loop with an index so you can look at `chain[i + 1]`.
Only compare when both timeouts are set.
template: Dojo.Eq("a healthy chain", new List<string>(), CheckBudgets(new() { ("client", 10000), ("gateway", 8000), ("integration", 5000), ("backend", 3000) }, 500));
Dojo.Eq("integration outlives the gateway", new List<string> { "integration (30000 ms) must be at most 4500 ms, inside gateway (5000 ms)" },
Dojo.Eq("margin matters", new List<string> { "backend (4800 ms) must be at most 4500 ms, inside integration (5000 ms)" },
Dojo.Eq("missing timeout", new List<string> { "backend has no timeout" }, CheckBudgets(new() { ("integration", 5000), ("backend", 0) }, 500));

steps.title: A deadline
prompt: The tests declare a clock you can control:
interface IClock { long NowMs { get; } void Sleep(int ms); }
class FakeClock : IClock { ... public void Advance(int ms) ... }
- `int RemainingMs`: budget minus elapsed, never below 0;
- `int TimeoutFor(int perCallMaxMs)`: the timeout to give the next call: the smaller of `perCallMaxMs` and the remaining time. Throw `TimeoutException` if the deadline has already expired.
hints: Store the end time (`clock.NowMs + budgetMs`) in the constructor.
`Math.Max(0, end - clock.NowMs)` keeps it from going negative.
template: Dojo.Eq("full budget at the start", 5000, dojoD.RemainingMs);
Dojo.Eq("first call gets its normal timeout", 3000, dojoD.TimeoutFor(3000));
Dojo.Eq("second call gets only what is left", 2000, dojoD.TimeoutFor(3000));
Dojo.Throws<TimeoutException>("no call after the deadline", () => dojoD.TimeoutFor(3000));
public long NowMs { get; private set; }
public void Sleep(int ms) { Sleeps.Add(ms); NowMs += ms; }
public void Advance(int ms) => NowMs += ms;
